summary: Provides background on large-scale Kerberos deployments in industry and identifies problems with the cross-realm authentication model of RFC 4120. It is a problem statement and is informational.

eli5.summary: Kerberos works like ID cards from one town, and this explains why it gets hard when towns must trust each other at large scale.

subtitle: Why authentication across organizational boundaries creates operational headaches.

tldr.problem: Large-scale industrial systems and enterprises need Kerberos authentication to work across separate administrative domains, but the current cross-realm model has serious limitations in reliability, scalability, security and performance.
tldr.mechanism: The document identifies six categories of issues that arise when realms form chains of trust for cross-realm authentication, ranging from unreliable intermediary authentication paths to computational performance bottlenecks on limited-capability devices.
tldr.outcome: This informational RFC defines the problem space and requirements but does not propose solutions, establishing a foundation for future work on improving Kerberos cross-realm operations.

today: RFC 5868 remains an Informational document that identifies problems in cross-realm Kerberos operations without proposing solutions. It has influenced later work on improving Kerberos deployments in large-scale industrial and enterprise systems, particularly regarding scalability and inter-realm trust management.

sections.title: The Cross-Realm Authentication Problem
sections.content:
Kerberos Version 5 is an authentication system where each managed domain, or realm, maintains its own database of users and shared secrets. When a user from one realm needs to access a service in a different realm, cross-realm authentication allows the two realms' Key Distribution Centers (KDCs) to cooperate.

In large-scale distributed systems, particularly industrial control networks, organizations split into multiple realms for geographic and management reasons. These realms then must authenticate each other to enable smooth operations. However, current Kerberos cross-realm operations introduce significant challenges that can affect performance, reliability, and security in these environments.
sections.eli5: Just like you might need a letter from your school's principal to prove you're a real student at another school, computers in different organizations need to prove they're trustworthy when talking to each other.

sections.title: How Kerberos Cross-Realm Authentication Works
sections.content:
In cross-realm authentication, users first contact their home realm's KDC requesting a Ticket-Granting Ticket (TGT) for use with the foreign realm's KDC. If the two realms share inter-realm keys (a direct trust model), the home KDC delivers the TGT directly.

When realms do not share keys directly, an indirect trust model is used. The home KDC provides a TGT that can be used with an intermediary realm that might share keys with the target realm. The client then iterates through intermediary realms until reaching one with keys shared with the target. This creates a trust chain between realms. Trust chains can be discovered automatically by following DNS domain hierarchy, but in many cases the chain must be specified manually.
sections.eli5: If your school doesn't directly know the other school, your principal might send you with a letter to a third school that knows both. That third school then sends you to the school you wanted.

sections.title: Requirements from Large-Scale Industrial Deployments
sections.content:
The RFC examines two actual large-scale petrochemical systems to ground its requirements: a centralized system with 16,000 devices across 3,000 network segments, and a distributed system with 26 geographically dispersed clusters containing 500-1,000 devices each. Industrial devices often have limited computational capabilities and power constraints.

Seven requirements emerge from these systems: (R-1 and R-2) support for multiple independent management domains and delegation between them; (R-3 and R-4) allowing device control across domain boundaries and geographic distribution within a domain; (R-5, R-6, R-7) reducing operational costs, limiting power consumption on device CPU, and managing limited bandwidth. These requirements frame what an improved cross-realm architecture must address.
sections.eli5: Real-world factories have thousands of machines spread out over huge areas, using simple computers that don't have much computing power. Any solution has to work with these real limits.

sections.title: Six Key Issues with Cross-Realm Operations
sections.content:
Unreliability of the authentication chain: If any intermediary realm in a trust chain becomes unavailable, end-to-end authentication fails, even if both endpoints' KDCs work perfectly. End-point realms have no control over or knowledge of intermediary realm health.

Man-in-the-middle attacks: Every KDC in an indirect trust chain knows the shared secrets between the client and remaining KDCs, allowing a malicious intermediary to intercept or forge messages and service session keys.

Scalability of direct trust: The direct trust model requires each realm to maintain inter-realm keys with every foreign realm it needs to interact with, growing maintenance costs exponentially with the number of realms.

Denial-of-service exposure: KDCs must be reachable across the network for cross-realm operations, opening them to public attack. Restricting access by IP prefix is not scalable when remote realms span multiple geographic locations.

Client performance: Clients must perform cryptographic TGS exchanges with every KDC in the trust chain. On limited-capability devices, this can introduce unacceptable delays, especially as trust chains grow longer.

Pre-authentication in roaming: Mobile clients cannot reach their home KDC to obtain credentials until they gain network access, but network access providers require valid credentials first—a chicken-and-egg problem.
sections.eli5: There are six big problems: the chain can break, someone in the middle can cheat, you need lots of secrets if realms talk to many others, KDCs get attacked easily, devices get slow with too much math, and roaming laptops can't log in to get on the network.

sections.title: Design Constraints for Solutions
sections.content: Any solution to cross-realm issues must carefully balance several constraints. Solutions should reuse existing Kerberos components and protocols rather than introducing entirely new ones. They should avoid requiring changes to already-deployed clients, since updating millions of client systems takes years. The burden on KDCs must be minimal, as KDCs are critical infrastructure. Solutions need not solve all six issues simultaneously, and different deployments may prioritize different requirements based on their environments.
sections.eli5: Whatever fixes these problems has to be smart about not breaking everything that already works, and has to work on computers that are already out there in the world.

references.text: Neuman, C., Yu, T., Hartman, S., and K. Raeburn, "The Kerberos Network Authentication Service (V5)", RFC 4120, July 2005.
